clue.text: Hero of Hemans ballad in Italian White House

bianca is the Italian (feminine) word for white

explanation.surface: A literary quiz question that seems to point to a grand Italian residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Italian' is a link telling you to translate, and Italian puts the adjective after the noun. The grid as filed shows the Moroccan city, one letter off.
explanation.definitionFit: Casabianca, the boy who stood on the burning deck, is the young hero of Felicia Hemans's famous poem.

clue.text: Torpor of Robin Cook?

definitions.meaning: the American author Robin Cook wrote the medical thriller of this title

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the second definition, a book by Robin Cook rather than a description of him; British solvers may think first of the politician of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep unconsciousness is an extreme torpor, and the word is also the title of Robin Cook's 1977 hospital thriller.

definitions.text: Dickens's reprieved gallows-bird, who kept his Grip

parts.words: Dickens's reprieved gallows-bird, who kept his Grip
parts.note: a Dickens title character condemned to hang and pardoned at the last, whose pet raven is named Grip

explanation.surface: A condemned man spared the noose who never lost his composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept his Grip' reads as keeping self-control, but Grip is the talking raven of the 1841 novel; a 'gallows-bird' is someone fit for hanging.
explanation.definitionFit: The simple-minded hero of Dickens's Gordon Riots novel is sentenced to death and reprieved, always with his raven at his side.

clue.text: Neckwear for R. L. Stevenson, for example

definitions.meaning: a broad cravat worn at the throat

explanation.surface: A question about what the author of Treasure Island wore round his neck.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as A SCOT for the second definition. ASCOT is also the name of a racecourse in Berkshire, England, whose formal dress gave the tie its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A wide silk tie looped under the chin is a kind of cravat; split in two, it names any native of Scotland.

clue.text: French dramatist takes encore ill (quite upset)

indicators.note: being thoroughly upset means these letters are tipped over into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A French playwright overcome by illness while taking a curtain call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite upset' rearranges the letters of ENCORE ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre Corneille, author of Le Cid, is one of the great tragic playwrights of seventeenth-century France.

clue.text: Present fears were less than horrible ones, Macbeth thought

definitions.text: Present fears were less than horrible ones, Macbeth thought

parts.words: Present fears were less than horrible ones, Macbeth thought
parts.note: Macbeth says 'Present fears are less than horrible' followed by the word wanted, his fancies of murder

explanation.surface: Macbeth reflects that what he dreads now is smaller than what his mind conjures.
explanation.walkthrough: From Act 1 scene 3 of Macbeth: the solver supplies the noun that 'ones' stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancies and fantasies conjured by the mind are what Macbeth finds more terrible than real dangers.

clue.text: Not Willie Loman, at all events, this novelist

definitions.text: Not Willie Loman, at all events, this novelist

parts.words: Not Willie Loman, at all events, this novelist
parts.note: Willie Loman of Death of a Salesman is a failing travelling salesman, so he is certainly not the top performer; the term also names a hugely popular book or author

explanation.surface: A remark that Arthur Miller's failing salesman is no successful novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Willy Loman, Arthur Miller's tragic salesman, sells badly; the answer reads as the most successful of sellers and also as a popular writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A novelist whose books sell in vast numbers is described by the same term as a top salesperson.

clue.text: Doric rimes possibly showing mercy

explanation.surface: Rhymes in a Doric dialect that display compassion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges DORIC RIMES. The word is Latin for pity, later a ledge under a choir seat and a dagger for the coup de grâce.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin misericordia, compassion; the old word survives as a term for pity and clemency.

clue.text: Sussex travel writer, but French

explanation.surface: A note on an English travel author with a French connection.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuart Petre Brodie Mais was a prolific English topographical writer, and his surname is also the French conjunction meaning however.

clue.text: Melville Levantine ceramicist?

explanation.surface: A Melville character imagined as a maker of pots from the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is just the author's name, standing for one of his novels (1855), whose hero is an American revolutionary soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Herman Melville's 1855 novel follows the wanderings of a Revolutionary War veteran of this name.

explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Fry's play hinges on the supposed transformation of the rag-and-bone man of this name.

clue.text: Playlet: one which failed, perhaps, as a curtain raiser?

definitions.text: one which failed, perhaps, as a curtain raiser?
definitions.meaning: a short piece that didn't work as an opener might be moved to the end of the bill instead

explanation.walkthrough: A curtain raiser comes before the main play; the joke is that one that flopped there might be shunted to follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Georgian theatre a short farce performed after the main play was called this, the opposite of a curtain raiser.

clue.text: From distant era, somehow, bad art detains. Due to contrary winds?

explanation.surface: Poor art holding up a traveller from a distant age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges ART DETAINS. The opening words as filed do not join the wordplay and may be OCR spill from another clue.
explanation.definitionFit: These upper-air currents blow opposite to the trade winds beneath them, hence the prefix meaning against.

clue.text: Saucy reminiscences from an enthusiast on New York eminence

explanation.surface: An admirer writing a racy memoir from a New York hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: John Cleland's 1748 erotic novel is subtitled Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleland's notorious novel is written as the bawdy memoirs of its heroine, a woman of pleasure.

explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible this young man is the fourth friend who lectures the suffering Job, a classic false consoler.
